newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER SHOWCASE-ENGLISH ECCENTRIC MEETS SCOTS GENT.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER SHOWCASE-ENGLISH ECCENTRIC MEETS SCOTS GENT.

text.p: When Hearts striker John Robertson had overcome the first wave of disappointment after losing 4-3 to Rangers in last month's Scottish League Cup final he sat down to write his regular newspaper column for the Scotsman newspaper.
"After being on the same pitch as Paul Gascoigne yesterday, I can't help but think that it is time for people to get off his back," he wrote.
"They can prattle on all they want about his private life, but his private life has got nothing to do with what happens on the football pitch and on a football pitch he is a genius.
"He showed two flashes of magic and produced two goals which saved Rangers. As a football player, the man is on a different level and that is how he should be judged."

Generous words from a man for whom Gascoigne's two goals, scored after Hearts had hauled themselves level from 2-0 down thanks to a Robertson equaliser, meant more of the same -- another trophy for Rangers, more heart-break for Hearts.
Robertson and Gascoigne, who are due to face each other again on Saturday in the latest clash between the two sides, come from different ends of the soccer spectrum.

Gazza, half-clown-half-genius, has dragged his talents from his native Newcastle to Tottenham Hotspur to Lazio and now to Glasgow, leaving a trail of wife-beating allegations, newspaper headlines and practical joke victims in his wake.

Robertson, apart from a brief spell on Gascoigne's home turf at Newcastle, has played for Hearts since leaving school, rarely grabbing the national headlines, constantly scoring goals and seldom causing offence.

Whereas Gascoigne has won the FA Cup with Spurs and the Scottish league title with Rangers, Robertson has yet to receive a winner's medal in a career spanning 16 years and including three cup final appearances.

Gascoigne has won 38 caps for England, shedding tears at the Italian World Cup in 1990 after a dramatic semifinal defeat by Germany, only to see the same thing happen again in this June's European championship.
Robertson, meanwhile, quietly chalked up 16 appearances for Scotland in a successful but unspectacular international career.
And while the England midfielder is notoriously erratic, the Scottish striker is a model of consistency, topping the individual scoring table at Tynecastle in every full season he has played there.
The two men do have one thing in common -- they have both been criticised for being unfit and overweight.
When Gascoigne was labelled a fat-so by the British press ahead of the European championship he responded as only he can, by leading England to victory over Scotland with a stunning goal at Wembley.
Robertson, a diminutive five-foot-six (167cm), responds with humour.
Asked about his physique in a recent newspaper article he laughed and gave an answer Rangers would be advised to heed on Saturday.
"Just remember," he said, "no game is over until the fat striker scores."
